nameStory: This tiny fungus gets its charming name because its fruiting bodies look exactly like miniature bird's nests complete with little 'eggs' inside! The scientific name stercoreus comes from the Latin word for dung, since this species has a particular fondness for growing on animal droppings.
description: The dung-loving bird's nest fungus is a fascinating tiny fungus that creates cup-shaped structures no bigger than a pencil eraser. Each little 'nest' is grayish-brown and contains what look like tiny eggs - these are actually spore-filled packets called peridiola. When raindrops hit the cup, they splash out these 'eggs' to spread the fungus to new locations. You'll typically find clusters of these miniature nests growing together on dung or dung-enriched soil.

idTips.label: Cup Shape
idTips.description: Small grayish-brown cups resembling tiny bird's nests, usually less than half an inch across, with smooth or slightly fuzzy outer surfaces

idTips.label: Spore Packets
idTips.description: Each cup contains several small, round, whitish to gray 'eggs' (peridiola) that look like tiny pebbles nestled inside

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Cups feel firm but delicate, with a slightly fuzzy or woolly exterior that becomes smoother toward the rim

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found growing directly on animal dung or soil heavily enriched with manure

idTips.label: Clustering
idTips.description: Typically grows in groups of many cups clustered together, rarely found as single specimens

habitat: Look for this fungus in pastures, barnyard areas, and anywhere livestock have been, especially on or near cow, horse, and sheep dung. It thrives in nutrient-rich soils around farms and can occasionally be found in heavily fertilized gardens or compost areas. The species prefers open, sunny to partially shaded locations where moisture can collect.

seasonality.spring: Young cup-shaped fruiting bodies begin appearing as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture for spore dispersal.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season when cups are most abundant and visible, especially after summer thunderstorms wash over pastures and manured fields.
seasonality.fall: Continued fruiting through early fall, though specimens may become weathered and less distinct as the season progresses.
seasonality.winter: Rarely visible in New England winters, though the fungus persists in the substrate and will resume fruiting when conditions improve.

funFact: This fungus has evolved one of nature's most ingenious spore dispersal systems - it literally uses raindrops as tiny catapults! When a raindrop hits the cup at just the right angle, it creates a perfect splash that can launch those 'eggs' up to 6 feet away.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relatives the fluted bird's nest fungus and field bird's nest fungus, but the dung-loving species is almost always found directly on or very near animal dung, while the others prefer rotting wood or plant debris.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bird's nest fungi,' these species have no special relationship with birds - the name comes purely from their appearance. The tiny 'eggs' inside are actually sophisticated spore packets that can stick to surfaces when splashed out by raindrops.
compareHints: Unlike the fluted bird's nest fungus which has distinctive ridges on the inside of its cups and grows on wood, this species has smooth-walled cups and grows on dung. The field bird's nest fungus is larger and typically found in gardens on plant debris rather than animal waste.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relatives the dung-loving bird's nest fungus (which prefers manure) and the field bird's nest fungus (which has smooth interior walls), the fluted bird's nest fungus is the 'fancy' one with decorative grooves inside and always grows on wood.
